tagline: Build a racing team, recruit and develop a young driver, test the car and earn prizes in official solo qualifying.
description:
Racelandia is a motorsport game for Game Hub in which you never steer. You run the team: you prepare the car, train the driver and read the weather, and the driver does the lap, because the lap is a real physical simulation.

The car has seventeen settings that all do something: front and rear wing, front and rear ride height, springs, anti-roll bars, camber, tyre pressures, brake bias, differential lock, gear ratios, engine mode and the fuel you start with. Aerodynamic downforce grows with speed, the floor loses its downforce if it touches the track, the tyres heat up, wear and lose grip outside their working temperature, and a badly set up car slides off the circuit. A good one takes the corners as it should.

Every visit has a time of day, and the weather of the day is the same for everyone: air and asphalt temperature, cloud, rain and a film of water on the track. Five tyre compounds, from soft to full wet, behave differently on a cold, hot, damp or flooded track.

New teams start with $5,000,000 and an empty garage. Buy a basic car for $1,000,000 and recruit one of three seventeen year old novices for $150,000, at most once every seven real days. Every skill starts at 50. Drivers age gradually: a seventeen year old reaches about forty-two after one real year, with physical decline beginning around thirty-two and no automatic retirement. Thirteen skills, from reaction time, reflexes and raw speed to braking, throttle control, consistency, concentration, mentality, tyre management, wet-weather driving, fitness and technical feedback, decide how the car is driven. They grow with seven training simulators you play yourself, such as the start lights, catching balls, holding a line, a braking point and a pit stop, so the driver reflects how well you play. Training uses driver energy without a monetary fee, and its difficulty gradually increases with the relevant skills. Skills also grow from driving laps.

Your car is made of parts: engine, gearbox, battery and energy recovery, brakes, suspension, floor and both wings. Every lap wears them, in practice too, and worn parts lose performance and can fail on the track. You repair them cheaper or replace them, and a heavy crash breaks several at once. The setup is kept separately for every circuit and remembered, and the garage lists what you tried before and the lap times it gave.

Practice tests the car and teaches the driver, with a $25,000 circuit fee plus tyres, laps and fuel, but no prizes. Official solo qualifying lasts 45 minutes, then finishes the current lap, under standard dry conditions. Weekend practices last 30 minutes. Its $60,000 circuit fee plus consumables and 25 energy buy a chance at bronze, silver or gold, based on the best three clean laps, consistency and valid-lap share. Prizes are $200,000, $260,000 and $320,000. Unused reserved laps are refunded. Sponsors pay $20,000 daily once the team owns both car and driver, with a qualifying bonus of up to $60,000 once per day. Three successful qualifying sessions, including silver or better once, earn a permanent license for future player races. Those races and driver trading are planned for later.

The replay runs in real time from a chase, cockpit, nose, TV, helicopter or free camera, with live tyre temperatures, fuel, energy recovery, and the three sectors coloured as on the timing screens: purple for the circuit record, green for your own best, yellow otherwise. While the car is on the track you can call it into the pit lane. The session clock keeps running while the car stands at its box; the stop opens with an analysis of the laps so far (balance, brake locks, wheelspin, tyre temperatures and wear per lap, how many laps the tyres have left) and ranges where each setup slider could move, which narrow with every lap of data. It slows to the limiter, stops at its box, and you can change tyres, wings, brake bias and more before it is released, and the stop costs real time. Every session is kept in the statistics with its laps, sectors, conditions and setup. Other players in the room appear as ghosts during tests; official solo qualifying runs alone.

Solo Division 5 adds a persistent 20-round championship against eighteen rivals that develop every real day. Every division needs two cars, each with its own driver, and Division 5 asks for level-20 cars and drivers averaging 55 or better, and a pit crew for each car whose speed decides every stop. Each weekend has three 30-minute solo practice sessions, a 45-minute solo qualifying and a twelve-lap race. Qualifying locks the setup until the race ends; tyres may still be changed. A weekend brings a fixed allocation of twenty tyre sets for all five sessions, paid once: six soft, four medium, three hard, four intermediate and three wet. A set keeps its wear from session to session, so you choose which new or used set to fit at the start and at every stop, in the sessions and in the race. Before the first practice the team gets a forecast with the chance of rain in each session. It is only an estimate: the further away the session, the less reliable it is, and it is refreshed after every session; the real weather of each session can differ. The practices measure how fast each compound wears and how many laps it should last, and the race shows each of the four tyres' wear, the laps left and the water on the track. The shared race model includes acceleration, traffic, overtaking, fuel, tyre degradation, pit stops and safety-car recoveries. Results, points, prizes, grids and standings are saved. Start sessions when you choose, with a real recovery interval between them that continues offline. Divisions 4 to 1 show their future requirements; their races, car upgrades and multiplayer races are not available yet.
capabilities: A physically simulated car: downforce, drag, ground effect, load transfer, tyre grip, tyre temperature and wear, fuel weight, brakes, differential and engine modes.
Seventeen car settings and five tyre compounds, remembered separately for every circuit, with a history of the setups you tried and the times they gave.
Eight parts that wear with every lap, can be repaired or replaced, break in a crash and can fail on the track.
Separate tests and forty-five-minute official solo qualifying: test for driver experience; qualify for bronze, silver or gold prizes, sponsor bonuses and a license for future player races.
A crash risk from driver error that falls as the driver's skills grow, and mechanical failures that grow with wear.
A circuit with a time of day, air and asphalt temperature, cloud, rain and standing water, the same for every player.

A young driver with thirteen skills that decide how the car is driven, starting at 50 and trained in six simulators (and a pit crew trained in drills of its own) that grow harder with their relevant skills, using energy without a monetary fee; a poor training session makes a skill a little worse.
Real-time pit stops: call the car in, it drives the pit lane and stops at its box, and you change tyres and settings before it is released.
Timing screens with three sectors coloured purple, green and yellow, a theoretical best lap, and statistics for every session.
Six cameras, a mini-map, live telemetry and a speed trace of your best lap.
Game Hub rooms for up to six players, with ghost cars during tests; official qualifying is solo and player races are planned for later.
An empty starting garage, a purchasable basic car, weekly youth recruitment, thirteen skills starting at 50, gradual aging and physical decline without automatic retirement.

Solo Division 5: two cars and two drivers, eighteen persistent rivals that train every day, a pit crew for each car, twenty rounds, three practices, qualifying with a locked setup, twelve-lap races, pit strategy, safety cars, saved results and championship standings.
Live timing for the eighteen solo rivals and your two drivers in practice and qualifying, with session best laps, leader gaps and a qualifying grid based on the same results.
A layered engine voice with combustion pulses, RPM crossfades, throttle load, gear-shift transients, intake and turbo sound, with a mute control in practice and races.
A weekend forecast with the chance of rain in every session, only an estimate that improves after each session, and real weather that can differ.

A fixed allocation of tyre sets for the whole weekend, with wear carried from session to session, chosen at the start and at every stop, and tyre notes from the practices (wear per lap and laps to the cliff).

A pit-stop analysis with lap-by-lap balance, brake and traction data, tyre temperatures and wear, and ranges for the setup sliders that narrow with every lap; the session clock keeps running while the car is in the box.
Thirty-minute practices and forty-five-minute qualifying; sector colours show one purple per sector for the fastest time of the session and green for your own best.
requirements: A browser with WebGL (3D graphics), which every current phone and computer has.

integrations.name: Game Hub
integrations.summary: Rooms and players run on Game Hub accounts: your profile, sessions, statistics and rating are recorded in Game Hub.
